overview: This is the atlas's 1492 to 1530 teaching label for parts of the archipelago. There was no country called the Philippines and no single archipelago-wide government in this period. The name Filipina was coined only in 1543, while the imported outline skips many major islands and must not be read as a real border.

periods.title: Trading communities and distinct polities
periods.summary: Ports, inland communities, datus and the Sulu sultanate belonged to overlapping regional networks rather than one Philippine state.

periods.title: Islamic polities and busy sea routes
periods.summary: Traditions place Sharif Kabungsuwan in Mindanao around 1515, while Sulu and many other communities followed their own authorities and histories.

periods.title: Encounter, alliance, coercion and Mactan
periods.summary: The Magellan-Elcano expedition negotiated and fought with several Visayan rulers; Lapulapu's forces defeated Magellan at Mactan, but the voyage continued.

periods.title: Local continuity after the expedition
periods.summary: The visitors departed and no Spanish colony followed during this card. The atlas endpoint is a data cutoff, not the fall of the archipelago's societies.

sections.title: Read the label before reading the history

items.text: The exact atlas record is id philippines, dated approximately 1492 to 1530. Those years describe imported map coverage. They do not mark national founding and extinction, because no state with this name governed the archipelago then.

The 1492 feature runs to 1500. It has eight separate polygons, 279 vertices and bounds from about 117.129 to 126.374 east and 5.488 to 18.552 north. Its many digits measure the file, not historical certainty.

The 1500 feature runs to 1530. It again has eight polygons and 279 vertices, with bounds differing from the first by only tiny fractions of a degree. That near repetition is a cartographic interval, not evidence that political borders froze for thirty years.

Point tests expose the outline's limits. Both versions include Manila, Vigan and Cotabato, yet omit tested points at Puerto Princesa, Iloilo, Cebu, Tacloban, Davao, Zamboanga, Jolo and Basco. The archipelago has become a map-shaped colander, so use it only as a locator.

The label is anachronistic. Villalobos applied Filipina to an island in 1543, after this card ends, and the name later widened to the archipelago. Using Philippines here is modern catalog shorthand, not the name people across the islands shared in 1492.

No matching Philippines feature appears at 1530 or 1600. A different record, philippines-1650, begins in 1650 and already has its own detailed card. The 120-year blank is an atlas gap, not a claim that people, ports or polities vanished.

There was no archipelago-wide capital or government. The NCCA account gives 1450 as the traditional founding date of the Sulu sultanate, but that chronology comes through genealogies and later historical reconstruction. It belongs in this story as a powerful southern polity, not as ruler of every island.

A separate NCCA survey says Muslim communities existed in Sulu by the late thirteenth century and attributes an early mosque tradition to Makhdum Karim in the fourteenth. Its words such as probably and attributed matter: perishable buildings and remembered genealogies do not behave like a modern dated registry.

The same institutional history places Sharif Kabungsuwan's arrival near Malabang in 1515 and calls a Maguindanao sultanate in 1516 possible. These traditional dates show political change within the atlas period, while their uncertainty prevents a pretend exact coronation calendar.

Underwater archaeology supplies a different kind of evidence. Wrecks at Pandanan, Lena Shoal and Santa Cruz carried ceramics from China, Thailand, Vietnam and Myanmar, plus metals, pottery, gongs, a weighing scale and even crocodile teeth. The sea joined communities that the map turns into isolated blobs.

The Santa Cruz wreck dates to 1488 to 1505, almost perfectly overlapping this card's opening. Excavators recovered about 15,000 objects, including thousands of intact ceramics, cooking pots, stoves, cauldrons, beads, bracelets and small cannon. Trade cargo carried both beautiful dishes and very practical kitchen hardware.

Older heritage gives the networks a deeper past. Butuan's lashed-lug boats date from the late eighth to early tenth centuries, and the Laguna Copperplate records a contract in an Early Kawi-related script in 900 CE. These discoveries show regional connections centuries before 1492, not one ancient Philippine nation.

sections.title: What archaeology can and cannot show

items.text: More than 1,000 burials excavated at Calatagan date around the fifteenth century. Their grave goods include local pottery, ceramics from China, Vietnam and Thailand, spindle whorls, ornaments, iron tools and shells. A single cemetery can therefore reveal trade, craftwork and mourning without telling us the deceased person's whole biography.

The Calatagan graves were unequal: some contained richer assemblages than others, part of a broader increase in burial stratification before 1521. Archaeology can reveal social differences, but grave wealth is not a tidy salary chart and should not be converted into fixed classes for every community.

Earthenware survives where words often do not. The National Museum collection includes cooking stoves and fourteenth-to-sixteenth-century Calatagan vessels. Shape, residue and find location help reconstruct cooking, trade and ritual, although no pot gets to stand up in court and explain who used it.

Goldworking was an old achievement rather than a gift of European arrival. Butuan objects date around the eighth century, and the National Museum places the strongest ornament tradition in the ninth to fourteenth centuries. Sixteenth-century Manila still had native goldsmiths, evidence of skills continuing into a changing world.

Fourteenth-to-fifteenth-century graves beneath Cebu's Plaza Independencia included rare gold covers for the eyes, nose and mouth. That is spectacular evidence from some high-status burials, not proof that everybody went to the afterlife wearing a shiny face mask.

One National Museum article uses a 1640 report and archaeological remains to discuss infant head shaping in parts of the Visayas. Because the written description is much later than 1530, it can only be a cautious clue about some childhood practices, never a rule for all babies in this card.

sections.title: The 1521 encounter was diplomacy and violence

items.text: Pigafetta was not an invisible camera. He took part in negotiations and joined the expedition whose actions he described. His manuscript was composed around 1525, after the voyage. It is precious eyewitness evidence, but its Christian labels and judgments reveal the author's position as much as local life.

Enrique of Malacca, an enslaved Malay-speaking interpreter, made conversations possible. Sources disagree on whether he came from Malacca, Sumatra or Maluku, and there is no sound basis for turning him into a secret Cebuano. Malay worked as a regional contact language among multilingual rulers and traders.

Humabon, ruler of Cebu, received the expedition on 7 April 1521. He permitted a cross and a Christian baptism ceremony, and he and members of his household took Spanish names on 14 April. Alliance, trade, religion and local rivalry became entangled within days.

The visitors also coerced. Pigafetta wrote that his group burned a neighboring hamlet because its inhabitants would not obey Humabon or the expedition. He later described threats against chiefs. Baptism and alliance cannot be narrated honestly without the guns, intimidation and destroyed homes beside them.

Lapulapu and his Mactan force rejected the attack. On 27 April 1521 they drove off Magellan's landing party and killed Magellan. Calling this a local victory is supported; pretending Lapulapu commanded a modern Filipino nation would put a later nation-state into his boat.

Pigafetta says Magellan's men burned twenty or thirty houses during the Mactan assault before retreating under fire. The battle was no clean duel between two famous men. It endangered residents, destroyed homes and involved large groups whose names the European account mostly did not preserve.

The alliance then ruptured. The NHCP chronology says Humabon supported the Mactan assault, faced a threat from Mactan afterward and led the killing of expedition officers at a banquet on 1 May. Local choices changed quickly after Magellan's defeat; no Spanish conquest followed in 1521.

The first circumnavigation did not end at Mactan. The Victoria reached Spain on 6 September 1522 after Magellan's death, with Pigafetta among eighteen returnees. The achievement belonged to a battered, multinational crew and depended on Asian interpreters, ports and provisions as well as European ships.

sections.title: Homes, food, dress, work and family

items.text: At Mazaua and Cebu, Pigafetta described wooden or bamboo houses raised on large posts and entered by ladders, with palm mats for sitting and sleeping. In one account animals stayed beneath the floor. The front door came with a short climb, but this eyewitness scene cannot define every island's architecture.

Coconut palms supplied drink, food, oil, milk-like liquid, vinegar, fiber for boat ropes and palm wine in Pigafetta's account. Rice, fish, pork, bananas, ginger and sugarcane also appear at meals or in exchange. One tree was doing the work of a pantry, bottle shop and hardware drawer.

Elite display could be dazzling. Pigafetta described a Butuan ruler with gold spots on each tooth, while archaeology confirms deep goldworking traditions. His smile could literally flash, but one ruler's dental fashion is not a population-wide description of health or wealth.

Tattooing existed before Spanish rule, but meanings and methods differed by community, age, gender and achievement. The National Museum's Kalinga discussion preserves that specificity. A modern child-friendly label such as cool body art would miss warfare, maturity and community identity embedded in the practice.

At Cebu's court, Pigafetta described embroidered cotton and silk on rulers, palm or bark cloth on other people, and young performers playing a drum and several gongs before a dance. This was one court scene through a visitor's eyes, not everybody's wardrobe or job. That much metal probably made whispering tricky.

A 1589 Spanish friar described Tagalog barangays as small groups led by datus, linked by kinship and friendship rather than one chain of command. He also recorded nobles, commoners, enslaved people and required service. This is later, Tagalog-focused and colonial evidence, not a template for Sulu, Cebu or every upland community.

The same late Tagalog account discusses marriage, inheritance, children and debt slavery, showing that households were legal and economic units as well as affectionate ones. Its categories came through a missionary writing for colonial officials, so children and enslaved people are heard mostly through an outsider with power.

sections.title: Learning, writing, health, water and toilets

items.text: A beautiful writing sample survives just after this card's period. The 1593 Doctrina prints ᜀᜋ ᜈᜋᜒ in Baybayin. Its syllabic reading is a-ma na-mi; the facing Roman text reads Amá namin, meaning Our Father. Traditional Baybayin normally left the final n sounds unwritten, so readers supplied them from language and context.

Baybayin is an Indic-derived alphasyllabary used by Tagalog speakers before Spanish arrival and afterward. The sample is a colonial Christian publication from Manila, sixty-three years after this card ends. It proves a writing tradition and adaptation to print, not one script, faith or literacy rate for the whole archipelago.

Pigafetta also wrote a 1521 Visayan word list in Latin letters. One entry is tubin, water; his editors compare it with tobig or tubig. It records a European ear and Italian spelling, not an Indigenous manuscript. Still, it lets a period voice peek through a very imperfect notebook.

No source used here demonstrates a standardized archipelago-wide school system in 1492 to 1530. Children likely learned many skills within households and communities, but that is an inference. The Baybayin print, trade weights, weaving tools and boat technology show knowledge; they do not give enrollment totals or a universal classroom.

Plasencia's later Tagalog account names ritual specialists and ceremonies seeking recovery from illness, safe childbirth and successful voyages. He called Indigenous religions devilish, so his categories need care. The evidence shows that health could involve ritual experts; it does not inventory medicines or prove identical practice elsewhere.

Pigafetta saw fresh water collected, coconut water offered and food prepared in earthen pots, but his surviving descriptions do not establish one water-supply system. Wells, springs, rain, rivers and carried water would have varied by island and settlement. A travel diary is a poor plumbing survey.

Toilets are the honest blank in this card. The museum earthenware summary identifies cooking and burial vessels, yet no securely identified household latrine or archipelago-wide waste system for 1492 to 1530. History cannot flush evidence into existence, so this card says unknown instead of inventing a bathroom.

A 1640 description says some Visayan families shaped infants' heads toward a locally admired form, and archaeology finds modified skulls in several central and southern sites. This is later and regional evidence. It reminds us that children had bodies, beauty standards and family care, while warning against one childhood story for thousands of islands.

sections.title: What came after the atlas stopped

items.text: The map ends at 1530, but no government called Philippines collapsed that year. Communities continued trading, farming, governing, worshipping and arguing. The empty 1530 and 1600 snapshots record a database gap, not an empty archipelago.
Villalobos introduced the name Filipina in 1543, after this card. That expedition did not create an archipelago-wide state; the name itself widened later.

Legazpi founded a permanent Spanish settlement at Cebu in 1565, outside this card. Spanish rule belongs in the separate philippines-1650 card, where colonial power, coercion and resistance can be explained at proper length.

U.S. colonial rule, Japanese occupation, independence, dictatorship and People Power are also outside a 1492 to 1530 record. They are important, already covered in the later card and should not be squeezed into a finale that makes four centuries look like an afterthought.

ending.text: In 1530 the atlas label simply stops. Distinct peoples, ports, sultanates, barangays and inland communities continued, and the very name Philippines still lay thirteen years in the future. The next atlas record starts only in 1650, after permanent Spanish settlement began, so continuity belongs to people and places rather than to one imagined state line.
